preamble.summary: Judith's victory hymn — the poetic crown of the entire book. This canticle recounts God's deliverance through Judith, celebrates the overthrow of the mighty by the weak, and ends with a cosmic vision of divine judgment. It is one of the finest examples of Second Temple praise poetry, standing alongside the Song of the Sea, the Song of Deborah, and the Magnificat.
preamble.remarkable: The hymn operates on multiple levels: personal thanksgiving, national celebration, and cosmic theology. It moves from the particular (one woman, one sword, one night) to the universal (God who judges nations and mountains tremble). The poetry deserves to be read aloud. The hymn has been set to music throughout Western history and remains part of the liturgy of the hours in Catholic and Orthodox traditions.
preamble.friction: The celebratory violence of the hymn — praising God for the destruction of enemies — reflects the lex talionis theology of its era and challenges modern sensibilities. It must be read within its literary and theological context as the voice of a community delivered from genocide.
preamble.connections: The hymn's closest parallels are the Song of Moses (Exodus 15), the Song of Deborah (Judges 5), Hannah's Song (1 Samuel 2), and Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:46-55). All share the theme of God reversing power structures through unlikely agents.

verses.text_latin: Incipite Domino in tympanis cantate Deo in cymbalis modulamini illi psalmum novum exaltate et invocate nomen eius.
verses.rendering:
Begin unto the Lord with tambourines,
sing to God with cymbals,
compose for him a new psalm,
exalt and call upon his name!
translator_notes: The opening echoes Psalm 33:3, 96:1, 98:1 — the 'new song' tradition. Judith's deliverance calls for new music, not recycled praise.

key_terms.note: The 'new song' demanded by new acts of salvation — a signature motif of the Psalter.

verses.text_latin: Dominus conterens bella Dominus nomen est illi.
verses.rendering:
The Lord crushes wars —
the Lord is his name.
translator_notes: Directly quotes Exodus 15:3 (LXX/Vulgate version). Judith places her hymn in the oldest tradition of Israelite victory poetry.

key_terms.note: The defining attribute: God is not a warrior-god who wages wars, but the God who ends them — who crushes war itself.

verses.text_latin: Qui posuit castra sua in medio populi sui ut eriperet nos de manu omnium inimicorum nostrorum.
verses.rendering:
He set his encampment in the midst of his people,
to deliver us from the hand of all our enemies.

key_terms.latin: castra sua in medio populi sui
key_terms.rendered_as: his encampment in the midst of his people
key_terms.note: God encamps with Israel — the Immanuel theology. His camp is stronger than Holofernes' camp.

verses.text_latin: Venit Assur ex montibus ab aquilone in multitudine fortitudinis suae cuius multitudo obturavit torrentes et equi eorum cooperuerunt valles.
verses.rendering:
Assyria came from the mountains of the north
in the multitude of his strength;
his host choked the streams,
and his horses covered the valleys.

key_terms.rendered_as: Assyria came from the mountains of the north
key_terms.note: The 'enemy from the north' is a prophetic archetype (Jeremiah 1:14, 4:6, 6:1) — the direction from which destruction always threatens.

verses.text_latin: Dixit se incensurum fines meos et iuvenes meos occisurum gladio infantes meos dare in praedam et virgines in captivitatem.
verses.rendering:
He vowed to set fire to my borders,
to slay my young men with the sword,
to give my infants as plunder
and my young women into captivity.

verses.text_latin: Dominus autem omnipotens nocuit eum et tradidit eum in manus feminae et confodit eum.
verses.rendering:
But the Lord Almighty brought him to ruin
and delivered him into the hands of a woman,
and she pierced him through.

key_terms.rendered_as: into the hands of a woman
key_terms.note: The refrain of the book distilled to its purest form — God's chosen instrument is female.

verses.text_latin: Non enim cecidit potens eorum a iuvenibus nec filii Titan percusserunt eum nec excelsi gigantes opposuerunt se illi sed Iudith filia Merari in specie faciei suae dissolvit eum.
verses.rendering:
Their champion did not fall by young warriors,
nor did sons of Titans strike him down,
nor did towering giants oppose him —
but Judith, daughter of Merari,
by the beauty of her face undid him.
translator_notes: The 'sons of Titans' and 'towering giants' invoke the mythological warrior tradition only to dismiss it. No epic hero was needed — only a beautiful widow.

key_terms.note: A rare Vulgate reference to Greco-Roman mythology, used to heighten the contrast with Judith's humble agency.

verses.text_latin: Exuit se enim vestimento viduitatis suae et induit se vestimento laetitiae in exultatione filiorum Israhel.
verses.rendering:
She stripped off the garment of her widowhood
and clothed herself in the garment of gladness
for the exultation of the children of Israel.

key_terms.rendered_as: garment of widowhood ... garment of gladness
key_terms.note: The clothing exchange as theological transformation — mourning to dancing, death to life (cf. Psalm 30:11).

verses.text_latin: Unxit faciem suam unguento et colligavit cincinnos suos mitra accepit stolam novam ad decipiendum illum.
translator_notes: 'Ad decipiendum illum' — 'to deceive him' — the hymn openly celebrates the deception. Beauty as holy subterfuge.

key_terms.note: The hymn makes no apology for deception — it is praised as divinely authorized strategy.

verses.text_latin: Sandalia eius rapuerunt oculos eius pulchritudo eius captivam fecit animam eius amputavit pugione cervicem eius.
verses.rendering:
Her sandals ravished his eyes,
her beauty took his soul captive —
the blade cut through his neck.
translator_notes: Three lines of devastating compression: sandals — eyes — beauty — soul — blade — neck. The seduction and the kill in a single breath. This is among the most celebrated tricolons in Latin biblical poetry.

key_terms.note: The sandals as starting point of the gaze that killed him — a small, feminine detail wielded as a weapon.

verses.text_latin: Horruerunt Persae constantiam eius et Medi audaciam eius.
verses.rendering:
The Persians shuddered at her steadfastness,
and the Medes at her daring.

key_terms.note: Two warrior virtues — constancy and audacity — attributed to a widow who never lifted a sword in battle.

verses.text_latin: Tunc ululaverunt castra Assyriorum quando apparuerunt humiles mei arescentes siti.
verses.rendering:
Then the Assyrian camp howled
when my lowly ones appeared —
parched with thirst.
translator_notes: The thirst-weakened Israelites terrify the mightiest army on earth. The reversal is complete.

key_terms.rendered_as: my lowly ones, parched with thirst
key_terms.note: The dehydrated defenders become the terror of the empire — weakness as the vessel of divine power.

verses.text_latin: Filii puellarum compunxerunt eos et sicut fugaces pueros percusserunt eos perierunt in proelio a facie Domini Dei mei.
verses.rendering:
The sons of young women pierced them through,
struck them down like fleeing children —
they perished in battle before the face of the Lord my God.

verses.text_latin: Hymnum cantemus Domino hymnum novum cantemus Deo nostro.
verses.rendering:
Let us sing a hymn to the Lord!
A new hymn let us sing to our God!

verses.text_latin: Adonai Domine magnus es tu et praeclarus in virtute tua et quem superare nemo potest.
verses.rendering:
Adonai, Lord —
great are you and glorious in your power,
and there is no one who can overcome you.
translator_notes: Jerome preserves the Hebrew 'Adonai' untranslated — one of the rare moments where the source language breaks through the Latin surface.

key_terms.note: Hebrew divine title preserved in the Latin — a mark of Jerome's reverence for the original.

verses.text_latin: Tibi serviat omnis creatura tua quia dixisti et facta sunt misisti spiritum tuum et creata sunt et non est qui resistat voci tuae.
verses.rendering:
Let all your creation serve you,
for you spoke and they were made;
you sent forth your spirit and they were created,
and there is none who can resist your voice.
translator_notes: The hymn expands from national victory to cosmic theology. God's creative word is the same power that defeated Assyria.

key_terms.rendered_as: you spoke and they were made
key_terms.note: Genesis 1 creation theology — the God who speaks the world into existence is the God who speaks armies into ruin.

verses.text_latin: Montes a fundamentis movebuntur cum aquis petrae sicut cera liquescent ante faciem tuam.
verses.rendering:
Mountains shall be moved from their foundations together with the waters;
rocks shall melt like wax before your face.

key_terms.note: Theophany language from Psalm 97:5, Micah 1:4 — even stone cannot withstand God's presence.

verses.text_latin: Qui autem timent te magni erunt apud te per omnia.
verses.rendering:
But those who fear you
shall be great before you in all things.

key_terms.note: The fear of the Lord — Judith's defining attribute (8:8) — now extended as promise to all the faithful.

verses.text_latin: Vae genti insurgenti super genus meum Dominus enim omnipotens vindicabit in eis in die iudicii visitabit illos.

key_terms.note: An eschatological horizon — the hymn moves from historical deliverance to final judgment, a rare apocalyptic note in Judith.

verses.text_latin: Dabit enim ignem et vermes in carnes eorum ut urantur et sentiant usque in sempiternum.
verses.rendering:
He shall give fire and worms into their flesh,
that they may burn and feel it forever.
translator_notes: This verse echoes Isaiah 66:24 and was cited by Jesus in Mark 9:48. It represents one of the clearest Second Temple expressions of eschatological punishment.

key_terms.note: The imagery of Isaiah 66:24, later quoted by Jesus (Mark 9:48) — eternal judgment upon those who war against God's people.

verses.text_latin: Et post haec omnis populus post victoriam venit in Hierusalem adorare Dominum et mox ut purificati sunt obtulerunt omnes holocausta et vota et repromissiones suas.
verses.rendering: After all these things, the whole people came to Jerusalem after the victory to worship the Lord, and as soon as they were purified, they all offered burnt offerings, vows, and their pledged gifts.

verses.text_latin: Porro Iudith universa vasa bellica Holofernis quae dedit illi populus et conopeum quod ipsa sustulerat de cubili ipsius obtulit in anathema oblivionis.
verses.rendering: Judith offered all the weapons of war of Holofernes that the people had given her, and the canopy she herself had taken from his bedchamber, as a votive offering of obliteration.

key_terms.note: The enemy's possessions are devoted to God — removed from human use, consecrated to divine possession, the memory of the tyrant erased.

verses.text_latin: Erat autem populus iucundus secundum faciem sanctorum et per tres menses gaudium huius victoriae celebratum est cum Iudith.
verses.rendering: The people were joyful before the holy things, and for three months the joy of this victory was celebrated with Judith.

verses.text_latin: Post dies autem illos unusquisque rediit in domum suam et Iudith magna facta est in Bethulia et praeclarior erat universae terrae Israhel.
verses.rendering: After those days, everyone returned to their own home, and Judith became great in Bethulia and was the most illustrious in all the land of Israel.

verses.text_latin: Erat etenim castitati adiuncta virtus ita ut non cognosceret virum omnibus diebus vitae suae ex quo defunctus est Manasses vir eius.
verses.rendering: For to her chastity was joined courage, so that she knew no man all the days of her life from the time Manasseh her husband died.

verses.text_latin: Erat autem diebus festis procedens cum magna gloria.
verses.rendering: On feast days she went forth in procession with great glory.

verses.text_latin: Mansit autem in domo viri sui annos centum quinque et dimisit abram suam liberam et defuncta est ac sepulta cum viro suo in Bethulia.
verses.rendering: She lived in her husband's house for one hundred and five years, set her maidservant free, and died and was buried with her husband in Bethulia.

verses.text_latin: Luxitque illam omnis populus diebus septem.
verses.rendering: All the people mourned her for seven days.

verses.text_latin: In omni autem spatio vitae eius non fuit qui perturbaret Israhel et post mortem eius annis multis.
verses.rendering: Throughout the whole span of her life, and for many years after her death, no one disturbed Israel.

verses.text_latin: Dies autem victoriae huius festivitatis ab Hebraeis in numero sanctorum dierum accipitur et colitur a Iudaeis ex illo tempore usque in praesentem diem.
verses.rendering: The day of this victory's festival is counted by the Hebrews among their holy days, and has been observed by the Jews from that time until the present day.
translator_notes: The book closes as it began — with a note about liturgical remembrance. The story exists to be retold, the victory to be re-celebrated, the God who saves through the humble to be perpetually praised.
